tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The neighbour who waters our plants is away this week.
The recipe which my aunt shared it needs less salt.
The library who opens on Sundays stays busy all day.
The bus that stops outside the school leaves at eight.
The park, that was closed after the storm, reopens tomorrow.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The neighbour who waters our plants is away this week.**

"Who" correctly refers to a person in a restrictive clause that identifies which neighbour we mean. The clause is essential, so there are no commas, and nothing else tries to occupy the subject slot.
**B) The recipe which my aunt shared it needs less salt.**

leftover "it" doubles the object after the relative has already taken that job. Repair: drop "it" — "The recipe which my aunt shared needs less salt." One object slot, one filler.
**C) The library who opens on Sundays stays busy all day.**

a library is a thing, so "who" is the wrong pronoun. Repair: "The library which/that opens on Sundays stays busy all day." Reserve "who" for people.
**D) The bus that stops outside the school leaves at eight.**

Restrictive "that" correctly defines which bus; no commas are needed because the clause is essential to identify it. The relative is the subject of "stops," and the sentence reads cleanly.
**E) The park, that was closed after the storm, reopens tomorrow.**

after commas (non-restrictive), exam English wants "which," not "that." Repair: "The park, which was closed after the storm, reopens tomorrow." Commas signal extra information — and "that" is not welcome there.
tasks.solution_overview:
These five sentences all turn on relative clauses that pick out a neighbour, a recipe, a library, a bus, or a park.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Ask whether the head noun is a person or a thing, and whether commas mark the clause as extra information. Also check that the relative pronoun itself fills the subject or object slot — no leftover object pronoun such as "it."

**Part 2: How to decide.**

In defining (no-comma) clauses, "who/that" fit people and "which/that" fit things. After commas, use "which" for things, never "that," and never leave a second object after the relative. Mark each sentence true only when those three checks all clear.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The chef whose soup won the contest teaches on Saturdays.
The cyclist who's helmet cracked bought a new one.
The concert, which sold out in an hour, starts at seven.
The students that organised the bake sale raised enough for the trip.
The garage, who stores our bikes, needs a new lock.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The chef whose soup won the contest teaches on Saturdays.**

"Whose" correctly shows possession: the soup belongs to the chef. You could rephrase as "the chef's soup," which is exactly what "whose" encodes in a relative clause.
**B) The cyclist who's helmet cracked bought a new one.**

"who's" expands to "who is," so "who's helmet" would mean "who is helmet" — nonsense. Repair: "The cyclist whose helmet cracked bought a new one." You need possession, not a contraction.
**C) The concert, which sold out in an hour, starts at seven.**

Non-restrictive "which" with commas correctly adds non-essential detail about a known concert. The commas tell you the clause is extra information, so "which" is the right pronoun for a thing.
**D) The students that organised the bake sale raised enough for the trip.**

Restrictive "that" for people is acceptable in defining clauses that identify which students. The clause is essential, so there are no commas, and the grammar stands as written.
**E) The garage, who stores our bikes, needs a new lock.**

a garage is not a person, so "who" is wrong. Repair: "The garage, which stores our bikes, needs a new lock." Places and buildings take "which," not "who."
tasks.solution_overview:
Here the focus shifts to possession, contractions, and the familiar who/which split across a chef, a cyclist, a concert, students, and a garage.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Separate "who's" (who is / who has) from "whose" (belonging). Keep "who" for people and "which" for places, buildings, and events — especially once commas mark a non-restrictive clause.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If you can rephrase as "X's Y," you almost always want "whose." Expand every "who's" before you tick true. For things with commas, expect "which"; for people in defining clauses, "who" or "that" are both acceptable.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The festival, that locals love, fills the square each July.
The tutor whom we hired last autumn still helps on Fridays.
The kettle which boils too slowly needs replacing.
The friend who we invited yesterday cannot come after all.
The photos that Maya printed them are still on the table.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The festival, that locals love, fills the square each July.**

a comma-bound clause must use "which," not "that." Repair: "The festival, which locals love, fills the square each July." The commas already signal that the clause is extra information.
**B) The tutor whom we hired last autumn still helps on Fridays.**

Formal "whom" correctly marks the object of "hired": we hired the tutor, so the relative stands for him/her. The structure is careful exam English and fully grammatical as written.
**C) The kettle which boils too slowly needs replacing.**

Restrictive "which" correctly defines which kettle; no commas are required because the clause is essential. British formal writing often prefers "which" even in defining clauses about things.
**D) The friend who we invited yesterday cannot come after all.**

Informal object "who" is widely accepted here: we invited the friend, and bare "who" as object is grammatical in modern usage. Exams may prefer "whom" after a preposition, but bare object "who" is usually fine.
**E) The photos that Maya printed them are still on the table.**

residual "them" doubles the object after "that" already stands for the photos. Repair: "The photos that Maya printed are still on the table." The relative already equals the object.
tasks.solution_overview:
This set mixes comma rules, object relatives (who/whom), and another leftover pronoun around a festival, a tutor, a kettle, a friend, and some photos.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Spot commas first — they ban "that" in careful exam English. Then ask whether the relative is the object of the verb inside the clause, and whether any residual "them/it" still sits where the relative already sits.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Non-restrictive → "which" for things. Object of "hired" can be formal "whom"; bare object "who" is usually accepted without a preposition. If the clause already does the object's job, delete any leftover pronoun before you mark true.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The runner who finished first still looked fresh.
The map that we borrowed shows every hiking trail.
The café whose windows face the river stays open late.
The singer who's opening the show arrives at six.
The film which the class watched last week was subtitled.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The runner who finished first still looked fresh.**

Restrictive "who" correctly identifies the runner; the clause is needed to pick out which person, so there are no commas. The relative is the subject of "finished," and the sentence is a textbook defining clause.
**B) The map that we borrowed shows every hiking trail.**

Defining "that" correctly restricts which map we borrowed. The relative is the object of "borrowed," which is a standard, fully grammatical pattern for things.
**C) The café whose windows face the river stays open late.**

"Whose" can mark possession for things as well as people: "the café whose windows…" means "the café's windows." The possessive relative is the right tool here.
**D) The singer who's opening the show arrives at six.**

"Who's" correctly expands to "who is" before "opening." Try the expansion in place — "the singer who is opening the show" — and the sentence still works, so the contraction is justified.
**E) The film which the class watched last week was subtitled.**

Restrictive "which" correctly defines the film the class watched. Either "which" or "that" works in defining clauses about things, and no commas are needed.
tasks.solution_overview:
All five sentences are clean models — use them as a reference sheet for people, things, possession, and a genuine contraction.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Confirm defining "who/that/which," possessive "whose" for a café's windows, and "who's" that really expands to "who is." Nothing here is trying to trick you with commas or leftover pronouns.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask person vs thing, then ask whether you need belonging or a contraction. If every piece fits — relative, head noun, and role inside the clause — mark true and move on.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The cousin with whom we share a flat cooks on Sundays.
The playlist, that includes every song from the trip, is private.
Anyone who's keys are missing should check lost property.
The museum which we visited last month displays local pottery.
The coach that designed the drills will explain them tonight.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The cousin with whom we share a flat cooks on Sundays.**

Preposition + "whom" is the formal, correct pattern when the cousin is the object of "with": we share a flat with the cousin. The structure is polished exam English.
**B) The playlist, that includes every song from the trip, is private.**

non-restrictive needs "which," not "that." Repair: "The playlist, which includes every song from the trip, is private." Commas + "that" is a classic exam fail.
**C) Anyone who's keys are missing should check lost property.**

possession requires "whose," not the contraction "who's." Repair: "Anyone whose keys are missing should check lost property." "Who is keys" is nonsense, so you wanted belonging.
**D) The museum which we visited last month displays local pottery.**

Defining "which" correctly identifies the museum we visited. Object relatives can keep "which/that," and the clause is essential, so no commas are required.
**E) The coach that designed the drills will explain them tonight.**

Restrictive "that" for a person is acceptable in a defining clause that identifies which coach. "Who" is often preferred for people, but "that" is not an error here.
tasks.solution_overview:
Preposition + whom, commas that ban "that," and another who's/whose swap sit across a cousin, a playlist, keys, a museum, and a coach.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

After a preposition referring to a person, prefer "whom." Commas still forbid "that" for things. Expand every "who's" before you mark possession true — "who is keys" never works.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan for a preposition immediately before the relative, then for commas, then for contractions. Defining "which/that" for places and people can stand when the rest of the grammar is clean.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The bakery from which we order bread raised its prices slightly.
The volunteer whom neighbours praised organised the litter pick.
The novel that Sam finished last night it still sits on the shelf.
Brighton, which hosts the festival, fills with visitors in May.
The friends who cake the party brought later left early.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The bakery from which we order bread raised its prices slightly.**

"From which" correctly links a thing after a preposition: we order bread from the bakery. Keeping the preposition with "which" is the formal pattern exams reward.
**B) The volunteer whom neighbours praised organised the litter pick.**

"Whom" correctly marks the volunteer as the object of "praised": neighbours praised the volunteer. If you can replace the relative with "him/her," "whom" is justified.
**C) The novel that Sam finished last night it still sits on the shelf.**

residual "it" doubles the object after "that" already stands for the novel. Repair: "The novel that Sam finished last night still sits on the shelf." One clause, one object slot.
**D) Brighton, which hosts the festival, fills with visitors in May.**

Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds a known fact about Brighton. Place names with commas almost always take "which," not "that," because the clause is extra information about an already-named city.
**E) The friends who cake the party brought later left early.**

word order inside the relative collapses — "who cake the party brought" is not English. Repair: "The friends who brought the party cake later left early." Keep the clause's internal order like a normal statement after the relative.
tasks.solution_overview:
Preposition + which, object whom, a residual "it," a city name with commas, and a collapsed word-order clause share the spotlight.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Keep the preposition with "which/whom" in formal answers. Delete leftover object pronouns. Rebuild any relative clause whose internal order has collapsed into nonsense.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read the relative clause as a mini-statement after the pronoun. If an "it" remains where that mini-statement already has its object, cut it. If word order inside the clause fails, rewrite it as a normal statement and only then judge the whole sentence.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The neighbour to whom the parcel was delivered signed for it.
The suitcase who's zip is broken stays in the loft.
Drivers whose licences have expired must renew them online.
The beach that we walked along at dusk was almost empty.
The headteacher, that announced the trip, answered questions calmly.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The neighbour to whom the parcel was delivered signed for it.**

"To whom" is the formal object pattern after a preposition: the parcel was delivered to the neighbour. Preposition + whom is almost always safe for people in exam English.
**B) The suitcase who's zip is broken stays in the loft.**

a suitcase's zip needs "whose," not "who's." Repair: "The suitcase whose zip is broken stays in the loft." "Who's" never marks possession — expand it and the error is obvious.
**C) Drivers whose licences have expired must renew them online.**

"Whose" correctly marks possession for people in a defining clause: drivers' licences have expired. The pattern works with plural noun heads just as with singular.
**D) The beach that we walked along at dusk was almost empty.**

Restrictive "that" correctly defines which beach we walked along. Object "that/which" can often be omitted in informal style ("The beach we walked along…"), but keeping "that" is fully correct.
**E) The headteacher, that announced the trip, answered questions calmly.**

non-restrictive about a person needs "who," not "that." Repair: "The headteacher, who announced the trip, answered questions calmly." Commas + person → who; commas + thing → which; never that.
tasks.solution_overview:
Formal "to whom," possession for things and people, defining "that," and a comma + "that" about a person are the checks in this set.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Preposition + whom is almost always safe for people. "Whose" marks belonging for licence holders and suitcase zips alike. Non-restrictive clauses about people need "who," never "that."

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Expand every "who's" before you mark true. If you see commas around a person's clause, demand "who." Defining object clauses with "that/which" can stand when no leftover pronoun appears.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The email which Jess sent yesterday still needs a reply.
The author of who the novel was written declined the interview.
The bridge that crosses the canal is closed for repairs.
Guests which arrive early may wait in the lobby.
The trainer whose tips improved my serve will join practice.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The email which Jess sent yesterday still needs a reply.**

Defining "which" correctly identifies the email Jess sent. Subject or object relatives both allow "which/that" for things, and no commas are needed here.
**B) The author of who the novel was written declined the interview.**

after a preposition referring to a person, use "whom," not "who." Repair: "The author of whom the novel was written declined the interview" (or, more naturally, rephrase to avoid the awkward passive relative). "Of who" is almost never correct.
**C) The bridge that crosses the canal is closed for repairs.**

Restrictive "that" correctly defines the bridge that crosses the canal. No commas appear because the clause picks out which bridge, and the grammar is clean.
**D) Guests which arrive early may wait in the lobby.**

guests are people, so "which" is the wrong pronoun. Repair: "Guests who/that arrive early may wait in the lobby." "Which" for people is a strong red flag in exam marking.
**E) The trainer whose tips improved my serve will join practice.**

"Whose tips" correctly shows possession: the tips belong to the trainer. "Whose + noun" is the clean possessive relative pattern for people (and things).
tasks.solution_overview:
People versus things and preposition + whom are the main decisions: an email, an author, a bridge, guests, and a trainer.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Defining "which/that" for things is fine. After a preposition referring to a person, never leave "of who" — raise it to "of whom" (or rephrase). Never use "which" for guests or classmates.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Label each head noun person or thing first. Then check any preposition sitting immediately before the relative. Possessive "whose + noun" earns an easy true when the belonging reading is clear.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The notes, which the lecturer circulated, summarise the chapter.
The applicant whom the panel interviewed withdrew this morning.
Anyone who's still outside should come in before the rain.
The app that tracks sleep was updated overnight.
The room in which the rehearsal takes place is on the second floor.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The notes, which the lecturer circulated, summarise the chapter.**

Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds information about known notes. If you remove the clause, "The notes summarise the chapter" still names a clear noun, so commas + "which" are justified.
**B) The applicant whom the panel interviewed withdrew this morning.**

Object "whom" correctly follows because the panel interviewed the applicant. Swap in "him/her": if that fits, "whom" is justified, and the sentence is careful exam English.
**C) Anyone who's still outside should come in before the rain.**

"Who's" equals "who is" before "still outside." Expand the contraction in place — "Anyone who is still outside…" — and the sentence still works, so keep "who's."
**D) The app that tracks sleep was updated overnight.**

Restrictive "that" correctly defines the app that tracks sleep. Everyday tech nouns follow the same who/which/that rules as any other thing.
**E) The room in which the rehearsal takes place is on the second floor.**

"In which" is the formal relative after a preposition for a place: the rehearsal takes place in the room. Formal writing prefers "in which" over a stranded preposition, though both can be grammatical.
tasks.solution_overview:
These mid-level models cover non-restrictive "which," object "whom," a genuine "who's," defining "that," and formal "in which."

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

If removing the clause still leaves a clear noun, commas + "which" are right for things. Object "whom" follows when you can swap in him/her. Formal place relatives often prefer "in which" over a stranded preposition.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Expand "who's" once — if "who is" fits, keep it. Treat ordinary tech nouns like any other thing for defining "that." Mark true when person/thing, comma pattern, and role inside the clause all agree.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The tent, that leaks in heavy rain, stays in the shed.
The clerk to who complaints should be sent sits at desk four.
Jars whose lids lack labels must be checked before use.
The witness who the lawyer called seemed unsure.
The recipe on which the cake depends needs soft butter.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The tent, that leaks in heavy rain, stays in the shed.**

** Commas + thing → which.

Trap: use "which" after commas. Repair: "The tent, which leaks in heavy rain, stays in the shed." Everyday nouns follow the same comma rule as any other thing.
**B) The clerk to who complaints should be sent sits at desk four.**

** Preposition + person → whom.

Trap: after "to," use "whom," not "who." Repair: "The clerk to whom complaints should be sent sits at desk four." Preposition + who is almost always wrong for people.
**C) Jars whose lids lack labels must be checked before use.**

"Whose" correctly marks possession for jars and lids: jars whose lids lack labels. "Whose" is fine for inanimate nouns in careful English, not only for people.
**D) The witness who the lawyer called seemed unsure.**

Object "who" is acceptable in modern usage for the person the lawyer called. Formal style may prefer "whom," but bare "who" as object — with no preposition before it — is not marked wrong in most exams.
**E) The recipe on which the cake depends needs soft butter.**

"On which" correctly attaches the preposition to a thing: the cake depends on the recipe. Keep preposition + which together in formal answers.
tasks.solution_overview:
Comma + "that," "to who," possession for jars, bare object "who," and formal "on which" are the five checks.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Everyday nouns still obey the comma rule — non-restrictive wants "which." Preposition + who is almost always wrong; raise it to "whom." "Whose" is fine for inanimate lids in careful English.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Fix person-preposition forms first, then comma + that errors. Accept bare object "who" in modern usage when no preposition sits before it, and reward formal "on which" when you see it intact.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The teammates with who we share a pitch signed the same form.
Edinburgh, which remains our favourite base, hosts the fringe each August.
The folder that Mia flagged contains old photos.
A classmate who's been seconded to the drama club still joins practice.
The prototype, which the lab tested last night, failed the heat check.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The teammates with who we share a pitch signed the same form.**

** with/to/for/by + person → whom.

Trap: use "whom" after "with." Repair: "The teammates with whom we share a pitch signed the same form." Any preposition before a person-relative wants "whom."
**B) Edinburgh, which remains our favourite base, hosts the fringe each August.**

Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds a known fact about Edinburgh. City names with commas take "which," not "that" or "who," because the place is already identified by name.
**C) The folder that Mia flagged contains old photos.**

Defining "that" correctly restricts which folder Mia flagged. Ordinary nouns follow ordinary relative rules, and the clause is essential, so no commas appear.
**D) A classmate who's been seconded to the drama club still joins practice.**

"Who's been" expands to "who has been," a correct present-perfect relative about the classmate. "Who's" covers both "who is" and "who has," and the expansion fits here.
**E) The prototype, which the lab tested last night, failed the heat check.**

Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds extra detail about an already-identified prototype. If the noun is already clear, commas + "which" are the pair for a thing.
tasks.solution_overview:
One clear "with who" error sits among solid city, folder, contraction, and prototype models.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Any preposition before a person-relative wants "whom." City names with commas take "which." "Who's been" can expand to "who has been," a correct present-perfect relative.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Find the preposition error first, then confirm each true sentence's person/thing choice and comma pattern. Non-restrictive "which" about an already-identified prototype is the expected pair with commas.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The guide through whom we booked the tour confirmed the time.
Parcels that arrive damaged must be photographed immediately.
The gardener whose allotment we admired stays on until dusk.
The schedule for which we planned the weekend has changed.
Someone who's coat is still hanging here left early.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The guide through whom we booked the tour confirmed the time.**

"Through whom" correctly marks a person after a preposition: we booked the tour through the guide. Booking and arrangement phrases often need "through/with whom."
**B) Parcels that arrive damaged must be photographed immediately.**

Restrictive "that" correctly defines which parcels arrive damaged. Everyday logistics nouns take the same defining "that/which" rules as any other thing.
**C) The gardener whose allotment we admired stays on until dusk.**

"Whose allotment" correctly shows possession: the allotment belongs to the gardener. "Whose" works cleanly before a concrete noun in a defining clause.
**D) The schedule for which we planned the weekend has changed.**

"For which" correctly attaches the preposition to a thing: we planned the weekend for the schedule. Prefer "for which" over informal stranded "which… for" in formal answers.
**E) Someone who's coat is still hanging here left early.**

** Who's + noun (possession attempt) → almost always replace with whose.

Trap: possession needs "whose," not "who's." Repair: "Someone whose coat is still hanging here left early." "Who's coat" expands to "who is coat" — never possession.
tasks.solution_overview:
Four solid preposition and defining patterns frame one "who's + noun" possession trap.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Through whom," "for which," and defining "that/whose" are trustworthy when the roles fit. The failing item misuses "who's" before a noun that needs belonging.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Expand the contraction in E — "who is coat" collapses immediately — then confirm the four true patterns: person after preposition, defining thing-clause, possessive whose, and formal for which.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The dentist by whom the filling was done explained the aftercare.
Players which miss warm-up cannot start the match.
A rule whose wording is unclear should be rewritten.
The hall at which we rehearsed drew a large crowd.
Anyone who's locker number is faded should ask at reception.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The dentist by whom the filling was done explained the aftercare.**

"By whom" correctly marks the agent in a formal relative: the filling was done by the dentist. The pattern is formal but grammatical, and exams accept it when asked for careful style.
**B) Players which miss warm-up cannot start the match.**

** Players/guests/classmates → who/that.

Trap: people need "who/that," not "which." Repair: "Players who miss warm-up cannot start the match." Never use "which" for players, guests, or classmates.
**C) A rule whose wording is unclear should be rewritten.**

"Whose wording" correctly marks possession for a rule: the rule's wording is unclear. Documents and rules commonly take "whose" in exam English.
**D) The hall at which we rehearsed drew a large crowd.**

"At which" correctly attaches the preposition to an event or place: we rehearsed at the hall. Prefer "at which / in which" in formal answers when the exam wants the preposition kept with the relative.
**E) Anyone who's locker number is faded should ask at reception.**

** Expand who's; possession → whose.

Trap: use "whose," not "who's." Repair: "Anyone whose locker number is faded should ask at reception." "Who's locker" expands to "who is locker," which never works.
tasks.solution_overview:
Formal "by whom" / "at which" sit beside a people-"which" error and another "who's + noun" fail.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Passive-related "by whom" and place "at which" are advanced but grammatical. Players are people — never "which." Documents can take "whose," and lockers need belonging, not "who's."

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Keep person/thing and contraction checks automatic at this level. Mark formal preposition patterns true when they fit; fail any which-for-people or who's-for-possession slip immediately.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The friend in whom's flat we stayed later moved abroad.
Few of the tools on which the repair depends are in the box.
The baker that her sourdough won prizes has closed for a week.
Neighbours whom the council thanked stayed for photographs.
The shed where tools are kept, that flooded last spring, is locked.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The friend in whom's flat we stayed later moved abroad.**

** Preposition + whose (+ noun), never whom's.

Trap: malformed possession — never stack "whom's." Repair: "The friend in whose flat we stayed later moved abroad." After the preposition, use "whose" to mark the flat as belonging to the friend.
**B) Few of the tools on which the repair depends are in the box.**

"On which" correctly links tools after a preposition: the repair depends on the tools. "The X on which Y depends" is a high-value formal pattern worth recognising on sight.

**Tip:** ** depend on → on which in formal relatives.
**C) The baker that her sourdough won prizes has closed for a week.**

** that her/his/its → whose.

Trap: replace "that her" with "whose." Repair: "The baker whose sourdough won prizes has closed for a week." "That + possessive" always signals a missing "whose."
**D) Neighbours whom the council thanked stayed for photographs.**

Object "whom" correctly refers to the neighbours the council thanked. Subject of the relative clause ("the council") + object relative "whom" is a clean formal structure.

**Tip:** ** Verb object is a person → whom is justified.
